reason: The sources provide over 15 corroborating facts detailing the scale, history, internal depth, and shrinking dynamics of Jupiter's Great Red Spot.
story: In 1831, astronomers confirmed the first undisputed sighting of Jupiter's Great Red Spot. This counterclockwise monster is the largest anticyclonic storm in the Solar System, with winds roaring past 200 miles per hour. Deep inside Jupiter's atmosphere, the vortex plunges roughly 250 kilometers down into the gas, insulated from friction because Jupiter has no solid surface. A century ago, this storm was colossal enough to swallow three Earths with room to spare. But continuous monitoring since 1878 reveals the giant is shrinking. Recent simulations show the storm feeds on smaller passing vortices like atmospheric prey; when that diet thins out, the spot contracts. In 2019, dramatic red flakes peeled from its edges, sparking fears the centuries-old storm was dying. Yet dynamicists insist its underlying engine remains intact. Even in its diminished state, the Great Red Spot remains wide enough to swallow our entire planet whole.
angle: Jupiter's Great Red Spot once swallowed three Earths side-by-side, and despite shrinking for a century, its 250-kilometer-deep vortex can still engulf our entire planet.

claims.claim: The Great Red Spot is an anticyclonic high-pressure storm system.
The storm is located in Jupiter's southern hemisphere.
The Great Red Spot rotates in a counterclockwise direction.
The Great Red Spot is the largest anticyclonic storm in the Solar System.
The first confirmed sighting of the modern Great Red Spot occurred in 1831.
Continuous annual observation records of the storm date back to 1878.
The Great Red Spot was historically large enough to fit three Earths within its boundaries.
The storm has been steadily contracting in size over the last century.
Internal winds around the edge of the storm exceed 200 miles per hour.
The storm's cloud tops rise roughly 8 kilometers higher than the surrounding Jovian clouds.
The storm extends downward to a vertical depth of approximately 240 to 250 kilometers below the clouds.
The Great Red Spot persists without dissipating partly because Jupiter lacks a solid ground surface to cause friction.
The storm is held at a consistent latitude by opposing eastward and westward jet streams.
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft captured the first detailed images of the storm during its 1979 flyby.
NASA's Juno spacecraft entered orbit around Jupiter in 2016 to conduct close-range passes of the storm.
In 2019, observers recorded large flakes and fragments peeling away from the edge of the storm.
The spot's red coloration is linked to solar ultraviolet radiation reacting with chemical compounds such as ammonium hydrosulfide and acetylene to form tholins.
Simulations using the EPIC atmospheric model suggest the storm shrinks when it is deprived of smaller feeding storms.
Planetary scientists compare the mechanics sustaining the Great Red Spot to high-pressure heat domes in Earth's jet streams.
The visual contrast of the Great Red Spot fluctuates in an inverse relationship with the South Equatorial Belt.

disputed: Whether 17th-century sightings by Robert Hooke or Giovanni Cassini represent the same storm: a 2024 study suggests the original spot vanished and the modern spot formed independently before 1831 (attribute as: 'historians debate whether 17th-century sightings were the same storm or an earlier predecessor that vanished').

Whether the storm will die within decades: some astronomers argued the 2019 cloud flaking heralded its demise, whereas fluid dynamics modeling indicates the underlying vortex remains intact and the flaking was merely surface interaction with adjacent cyclones (present as an ongoing scientific debate).

Current size relative to Earth: older sources describe the spot as twice Earth's size, while recent measurements show it is just over 1 to 1.3 times Earth's diameter (specify that it has contracted from three Earths wide down to just over one Earth today).
